utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Although we still have to deal with a few exhibits, the Chamber prefers to start first with the next witness. Mr. Tieger, will it be you who takes the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And are you ready to call the witness, which I understand is Mr. Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that there was quite a large number of documents which were related to, attached to the 92 ter statement. Mr. Registrar is preparing to provisionally assign numbers to those documents. Were there any objections? I have seen from written submissions that neither against the 92 ter statement nor against any of the exhibits there seem to be objections. Is that well understood? Mr. Kuzmanovic, you're nodding yes, together with Mr. Mikulicic. Same for the Gotovina Defence, yes, and for Cermak as well. Then, Mr. Registrar, since there are no objections, you can fully number through the list of exhibits, which we find in our Excel sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Forand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Forand, before you give testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Forand. Please be seated. Mr. Forand, I address you as Mr. Forand rather than as General Forand. That is not in any way out of disrespect for the rank you -- you hold or you held, but it is mainly to emphasise that everyone who testifies in this courtroom comes as -- despite whatever his rank or position is to come and tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Other may choose to do otherwise, but this is what the Chamber does, but I just wanted to make sure that you do not understand this to be in any way disrespectful behaviour. You will first be examined by Mr. Tieger who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General Forand.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to begin very simply by having you state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Alain Forand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And General Forand, I'd like to run through quickly through some of the highlights of your military career. Let me note preliminarily that I'm sure it won't be exhaustive or comprehensive, but just I want to provide the Court with some sense of your background. If I may, I'll just recite some of what I understand to be the highlights, and if you can just affirm that as accurate or not. You joined the Canadian forces in September 1967 in -- or by July of 1976, you had been chosen as the ADC as the Commander of the Mobile Command. Prior to that, you had served twice in Cyprus, one during the course of the 1974 hostilities. You were promoted to major in August of 1978 and commanded B Company 1st Battalion until 1980. You served as a chief instructor at the infantry school in the Canadian forces base, Gagetown. In 1982, became commanding officer of the 3rd Battalion. In July of 1987, became senior staff officer operations and training at mobile command headquarters. In 1988, you were director of military operations coordination and after that, director of military plans coordination. In 1993, you were promoted to the rank of brigadier-general, and in 1995 in approximately end of June and beginning of July 1995, in you assumed command of the United Nations peace-keeping force in Sector South as UNCRO commander for Sector South. Is that correct, General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would only add that I commanded my brigade in Quebec from '93 to '95, and I received the Star of Courage for action under fire in saving two of my soldier in Cyprus in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, General, you have provided the Office of the Prosecutor with four statements dated 19 and 20 June 1996; June 6, 1997; November 1999; and January 2008; and I'd like to ask if you reviewed those statements before coming to court this morning?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I understand, General, that in the course of that review, you identified a few corrections you wanted to make, and I would like to run through those briefly with you. First, there's a reference on page 6 of your 1996 statement - that would be 5 of the B/C/S - to more than 1.000 refugee in the UN HQ compound and that I believe you wanted to indicate to the Court that your recollection is that there were approximately 700 plus refugees in the UN HQ compound and that the reference to 1.000 reflects the total number of refugees who left Knin on September 16th, 1995. Second, you wanted to correct a reference in your 1997 statement at page 12 in the English, page 7 in the B/C/S, to the number of bodies you observed in Knin on August 5th, 1995. And you wanted to indicate to the Court that you believed that the number of bodies was 22 as reported during your 1995 interview you gave and in your 1996 statement at page 7 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S. Next, you identify a reference to a trip to Kistanje contained in your 1997 statement at page 14 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S, and wanted to indicate to the Court that although you did travel through Kistanje at some point and witnessed people looting in the presence of soldiers and military police and also observed considerable damage to the town either from shelling or burning, that you -- that this did not occur on the 12th of August, which was the day on which you travelled to Donji Lapac. Next, you wanted to indicate that the reference to the duration of shelling in -- at paragraph 5 of your 2008 statement should be modified and that you recall that the steady shelling that commenced on the morning of 4 August lasted for approximately 45 minutes to an hour, and thereafter, intermittent shelling continued throughout the day. You wanted to indicate a reference at paragraph 12 of your 2008 statement to visiting the parliament building and the RSK Ministry of Defence and wanted to indicate that you only visited the RSK Ministry of Defence on that day twice, which you recalled as being a three-storey building on the main road in Knin. And finally, you wanted to offer a correction to the number of troops to the UN battalions and companies, which are found at paragraph 2 of your 2008 statement, and the correct numbers you wanted to indicate to the court are as follows: The Kenyan battalion had 1.060 troops; Canadian battalion, 761; Jordanian battalion, 1.245; Czech battalion, 825 troops; the Indonesian medical company, 56 troops; the Czech medical company, 21 troops; and the Slovenian engineering company had 64 troops. General, with those corrections, do the statements, the four statements from 1996, 1997, 1999, and 2008 accurately reflect what you told the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that information truthful and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you to be asked about the same matters here in court today, would the answers you provided -- the information you provided be the same?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: They would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would tender those statements. I believe those are 65 ter numbers, 4944 through 4947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have not asked the witness to identify the statements, but think that is a formality rather than, Mr. Tieger, I take it that you took the witness through exactly the same statements as you're tendering now. So, therefore, there should be no doubt as to -- may I take it that Defence agrees with that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, we start with the 1996 statement of Witness Forand would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's 65 ter 4944 and becomes Exhibit P330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P330 is admitted into evidence. Then we come to the 1997 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 4945 becomes Exhibit P331.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P331 is admitted into evidence. The 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 4946, and it becomes Exhibit number P332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P332 is admitted into evidence. Finally, the 2008 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 4947 and becomes Exhibit P333.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P333 is admitted into evidence. Before we continue, Mr. Tieger, there's still one decision to be taken in relation to exhibits, and that is adding four new exhibits to the 65 ter lists. These are the -- the daily sitrep Sector South of the 20th of August. The other one is the daily sitrep of the 23rd of August; and then human rights issues, needs for action by Croatian authorities, 3 September 1995; and finally, the fourth is a letter, Cermak to Forand, dated the 8th of August copied to Gotovina and Reljic. In the written submissions, I did not find any objections against adding those exhibits to the 65 ter list. Therefore, your request is granted. These four documents are now added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And in light of the Court's comment about the formality of observing the statements - much appreciated, by the way - I should note that I believe I misspoke in identifying the first statement. If I recall correctly, I think I said it was the 19th and 20th of June 1996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it was August. Yes, the 65 ter number was right, but I noted that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour, and if I may, at this point I'd like to read a brief summary of the witness's statements, obviously not attempting to encapsulate all details but the normal summary. We read in -- I'm not sure if I actually explained that process to the witness, and I apologize for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will briefly do that. Mr. Forand, since large parts of your evidence are submitted in a written form, the public who is following these proceedings is not aware of the content, and therefore those portions of the evidence that are submitted in written form, usually a summary is read by the party who presents this evidence. So that's what Mr. Tieger will do that now. Just listen to your own -- to the content of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Witness 115, General Forand, arrived in Knin on approximately 1 July 1995 and was the UNCRO Sector South commander stationed in Knin from approximately 8 July 1995 until October 1995. He authenticates numerous Sector South sitreps and other documents that he sent and received during his period of command. General Forand observed and assessed the shelling of Knin on the 4th and 5th of August, 1995, and the resulting flight of the civilian population. Based on his observations, he concluded that the shelling was indiscriminate and directed against the civilian population to create mass panic and sent a letter of protest to General Gotovina. He also met with members of the RSK leadership on the evening of 4 August 1995, who discussed with him evacuating civilians from Knin and the surrounding area but had no plan to implement it. General Forand observed convoys of civilians on the evening of August 4th, 1995, moving out of Knin and moving from Drnis through Knin and to the north. On the evening of 4 August 1995, General Forand allowed the crowd -- allowed a crowd of refugees who had gathered at the front gate of the UN compound in Knin into the compound to protect them from the artillery attack. General Forand will describe being locked down in the compound by the Croatian army for three days after it entered Knin commencing on 5 August 1995 while looting and burning was taking place, and he will describe continuing restrictions of movement for UN personnel who were attempting to assess whether human rights violations were occurring. General Forand observed evidence of and received reports of looting, burning, destruction, and killing by Croatian forces in the days following Operation Storm. Widespread criminal activity continued despite the numerous protests by the witness during his meetings and communications with, in particular, General Cermak. General Forand also had two meetings with General Gotovina after Operation Storm, during which he complained to General Gotovina about the lack of discipline of his troops and the looting and arson taking place. That concludes the summary, Your Honour, and I will begin to -- begin the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, I'd like to take you a time before some of the events mentioned in that summary, and I'd like to direct your attention to roughly the time of your arrival in the sector, and I understand from your statement, and I believe that is found at -- the June 1997 statement at page 2 and also page 2 in the B/C/S, page -- pages 2 and 3 in the B/C/S that you met General Gotovina on two occasions before the commencement of Operation Storm. Now, you had described the first as a sort of get-acquainted meeting and also indicated that at both meetings the issue of the shelling of the area around Cetina and Vrlika from the Dinara mountains by HV and HVO forces same up. You indicated in your 1996 statement at page 2 that this was an agricultural area of mostly farmers and that the shelling occurred while people were harvesting and that it made it dangerous for them to collect crops. Now, if I can just direct your attention to those meetings, can you explain to the Court the -- your concern or your predecessor's concern about the shelling that was taking place in the Cetina area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Certainly. At the first meeting, it was General Kotil that was still the commander of Sector South. I was accompanying him because it gave me the opportunity to meet General Gotovina who was the commander of one part of my -- of the Croat force, you know, on the -- a portion of Sector South. This shelling in the Cetina area was brought to -- by General Kotil to General Gotovina at that first meeting. Following that first meeting, I sent, if I remember well, two letter to General Gotovina regarding also the shelling in the Vrlika and the Cetina area, and I requested a meeting with General Gotovina, which if I remember well took place on the 19th of July where there was two points that I want to brought to him; one was the continuous shelling, which was creating problem for the farmers. They were not able to collect what was on the ground; and the other thing was I wanted to explain to General Gotovina what was my intention because my intention was to put more observation post in the Dinara mountain because of the problem that were in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you mention two letters of protest. You have a binder in front of you. That should make it easier to access some of those documents, although they will be shown on the screen. And if I could call up first 65 ter 490. That is found in tab 5 of your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this sufficient for the registrar to know what is to be brought on the screen? Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have 65 ter number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we discussed that in advance and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If it is well organised, then I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a letter dated July 9, 1995, to General Gotovina signed by you. It is a protest of the HV/HVO shelling west of the Dinara mountains. And you refer in the first paragraph to rounds which were fired on July 5th and also refer to a similar incident from July 1st, which you had also brought to the General's attention the following day. Is this one of the letters prompted by the information you were receiving about the shelling in the Cetina area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, this is -- was one of the area. On the 1st of July, I didn't sign that letter. It was General Kotil. When we met with General Gotovina the first time, he denied, you know, that he had any troops on the Bosnia-Herzegovina area, that it was not his troops, you know, that was firing into that particular area. That's why if you see, you know, I sent a letter to General Gotovina but also to Major-General Blaskic, which we thought at that time, you know, was the individual responsible of the HVO in the Livno valley. And I also went, you know, into that particular area to look at what was happening there, and I saw the damage that had been inflicted by artillery, and I ordered the Kenyan battalion, which was responsible for that area, to augment their patrol, and that information was passed to General Gotovina, so that it would put a bit of a refrain, you know, on whoever, you know, was firing onto that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me ask you, General, to look at the next tab, tab 6. That would be 65 ter 3300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, we'll refrain from assigning numbers and admission because these are all on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. These have all been admitted now, and I know that the -- my understanding was because of the number of document it is would be a logistical exercise for the registrar, and I think we concluded it would be preferable to continue to -- and easier for all parties to continue to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we will not at this moment bother about numbers because that will come up once the registrar has finished his job to assign numbers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this document, 65 ter 3300, is a letter dated 12 July 1995, again, from you to General Gotovina and again protesting the HV/HVO shelling west of the Dinara mountains. And it indicates that the UN observed on July 9th 42 artillery rounds and six rounds believed to have been from a tank fired from the heights of the Dinara mountains under HV/HVO control. You refer back in the remainder of the paragraph to similar incidents earlier that month but also note that this latest incident resulted in the injury of four non-combatant civilians and the destruction of four homes in an area devoid of military targets. And, General, was this the other letter you indicated you had sent prior to the second meeting with General Gotovina that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned a -- that that meeting occurred to the best of your recollection on July 19th, 1995. There's a document that has already been admitted into evidence here in this courtroom, and that's D157, and it is found at tab 8 of your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document which was apparently prepared and signed by Assistant Commander for Political Affairs Captain Tomasovic from the Split Military District, and I take it that you did not see this document at the time it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- but have you had an opportunity -- have I provided you with an opportunity to look at before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention in particular to page 2 of the document, which in the middle part of the page indicates that during the course of further discussion there was a -- further discussion as it says here that was based on the points of the letter by UNCRO delivered to the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina. And he responded, and there's a paragraph which describes General Gotovina's response, both in respect of the area Cetina, and then it goes on to discuss the children's camp at Karin Beach where UNCRO was requesting guarantees from the Split Military District there would be no combat are -- combat activity toward the area of the children's camp. General, can you tell us having had a chance to look at that document whether it refreshes your recollection of the discussion with General Gotovina or in any respects in which you can assist the Court in the issues discussed at that portion of the letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt. With regard to this, looking at the supplemental information sheet which is designed to supplement that information we received to date, there's no information contained in that supplemental information sheet concerning discussions of this document or matters contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, Your Honour, and should the witness testify to -- I mean, it's a discretionary matter for the Prosecution in terms of I think the notice necessary to proceed. I'm not -- I think there's been discussion about the nature of the supplemental information sheet before, and it's logistically impossible for it to be an exhaustive -- nor is there any purpose for it to be an exhaustive account of everything that takes place during the proofing session, and I don't anticipate that there's anything that will arise from the discussion concerning this document that will be problematic for the Defence to deal with, and as a matter of notice, if there is we can deal with it accordingly, and I'm sure the Court would afford the Defence sufficient time to deal with it. And I will say if it's determined to have been some kind of oversight, I apologise in advance. We're trying to deal with a number of issues, and I don't anticipate this presents any kind of problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber will not prevent you from putting these questions. At the same time, you're urged to be as complete as possible in disclosing to -- to the Defence teams what you dealt with during the proofing sessions, which is not just literally repeating what the statement say already. At the same time, Mr. Kehoe, if the matters raised now would ask for additional time to prepare, then please let us know that and why and what you exactly would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I believe I had asked you to look at that portion of the D157 and assist the Court if possible with your recollection of that meeting and any aspects of the exhibit that you can shed light on.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yeah. To the best of my recollection, this described the point that were discussed at that particular meeting. Regarding the children camp at Karin Beach, that was part of the confidence-building measure that we wanted to establish by providing, you know, for the children in the Krajina side, you know, with some opportunity to have fun. Regarding the border incident that was taking place, all I can say is that following the 12th of July letter there was a period of about two weeks where no shelling took place. That's all I have to say on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, were you ever made aware of -- from any of the UN elements patrolling the area of Cetina of Serb weaponry or artillery fire from -- in the area that was being shelled by the HV/HVO and in particular in the area where the harvest was being prevented?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having seen the situation report that indicate that the artillery fire were firing from that particular location, and when I went and visited in the Vrlika and Cetina area, the Kenyan soldier that were there never alluded to that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever -- when you visited, did you see any evidence of Serb weaponry or positions in the area where the shelling was taking place or where the harvest was being prevented?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, I did what I would think or qualify as a complete tour of the area, and I didn't see none of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive or learn about a formal protest by Croatian authorities about an alleged cease-fire violation consisting of Serb shelling from the areas mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Of shelling, no, but I think there was a report somewhere in July about some shooting originating from the Serb side but no artillery shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say shooting but no artillery shelling. Does that mean small-arms fire of some sort?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that is what that sitrep indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, I would like to turn next to August 4th, 1995, and the commencement of Operation Storm on that date. You've indicated in your statements that the attack began with shelling at precisely 5.00 on that date. I'd like you to turn, please, to tab 4 of your binder -- sorry, I apologise. Tab 11. And that would be P83.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If that could be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tieger. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Did we get provided a binder with these tabs, or is it just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is just -- this is just to expedite the examination process. I could wait until the document comes up on the screen as it does for all of us, but I thought it might be slightly faster if the witness had the binder. I -- if you're concerned that the documents in the binder conform with the documents on the screen, I can certainly ask the witness to check the screen periodically to make sure that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that is Mr. Kuzmanovic' concern but just whether -- I think what Mr. Tieger does is to assist the witness in quickly finding in the binder the document, whereas we have, perhaps, also, in order to save paper and hard copies for us to use our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a problem, Your Honour. I just thought it would be easier for all of us to follow at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it takes half a wood to have these binders copied for all of us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, P83 is a document dated August 4th, 1995. It's a -- headed "Protest, Attacks on Innocent Civilians and UN Installations" dated August 4th, 1995 and signed by you. And, General, can you tell the Court, please, when and why you sent this document?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. I was advised at 3.20 in the morning, you know, that in all probability the Croat would launch the offensive. We had been forewarned a couple of times before that, and potentially because we knew that the -- the discussion at Geneva, you know, had not gone well that this time there could be exact. So I immediately decided to start to recall and advise all of my unit, and that was state red, which put them at full alert. Everything was completed at 3.40. Then I moved to my headquarter in Knin because I was living within Knin itself. At 5.00, we start -- that's where the shelling started and heavy shelling that started. I immediately went on the balcony on the third floor. My office was opposite on the third floor, and what I saw was -- what I felt, you know, was indiscriminate shelling because I a knew a little bit about Knin even though I had been there only a month before it happened. There were five or six other officers with me on the balcony, officers who had been in the area for four to five months and knew Knin much better than I, and we didn't see the round landing, but we could see the puff of smoke, and it seemed to me in the comment they were making that it was not only directed at what would be military target but within, also, the civilian population. I stayed about ten minute at the most, you know, looking at the artillery barrage that was taking place. Then I went down to my operation centre to start to get some information of what was happening throughout my area of responsibility, and the information we were getting back from the headquarter of my unit, I had four unit under my command, were similar where there was some artillery fire in the -- near the zone of separation where the Serb defensive position but also within towns, and it seemed to those that were observing that shelling that it was also indiscriminate because in their view there was no military target there. So as the information was continue to be provided to me, I decided to write that letter and send it to General Gotovina and General Norac, the two Croat officer that I felt were responsible, within my sector to tell them that this was happening and from my point of view it was indiscriminate shooting and that they should stop it immediately. Now, I -- we had the military observer that was in Gracac -- correction, in the -- in Zadar, where General Gotovina headquarter was, and I made sure that when that letter was sent I told it -- it was either to Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk or Major Balfour - Lieutenant Tymchuk was my senior liaison officer; Major Balfour was my senior ops officer - to ensure that it was received by the military observer and that it was passed on -- ensure it would be received by General Gotovina, and they came back later, and he says, yes, the fax has been sent, it has been received, and a couple of -- an hour, maybe later, I was told that, yes, it had been given, you know, to Captain Nevi Jekovik [phoen], if I remember the name right, who was working directly for General Gotovina. So that's what happened, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned observing the portions of the -- or a portion of the initial period of the shelling of Knin. First of all, can you give the Court any indication of the intensity of the fire during the first period of shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, I would -- what I call -- I'm not a total expert, but I had seen some shelling being done before in Cyprus in '74 during the Turkish invasion. I would call it, you know, during the first 45 minutes very intense. At least the ten minute I was on the -- five to ten minute I was on the balcony it was extremely intense in the sense that it seemed that it was a battery, six-gun, at every location because of the sound we were hearing. So it was all over the place to me, it seem, what I would qualify as intense shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the concept of adjusted fire?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you observe any adjustments of fire during the course of your observations of the shelling on the morning of August 4th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No. The five to ten minute I was there, to my view there was no adjusted shelling. You know, it just -- the intense fire shelling began immediately. There was no adjustment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. General, I want to next direct your attention to the -- let me ask you, sorry, one more question about the -- the letter you sent. It mentions a number of towns, Drnis, Medak, Brunic, Benkovac, and Kistanje. Were these the only towns about which you received information that day that were the subject of shelling and specifically, shelling of civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No. If I remember well, there were -- the majority of all the town, you know, that was adjacent to the zone of separation also were under artillery fire, but I only decided to list, you know, the major town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I indicated that I wanted next to draw your attention next to the period of time after Croatian forces entered Knin. Let me ask you preliminarily whether the successful -- whether Operation Storm and the re-taking of the Krajina by Croatian forces changed the mission of UNCRO in your view and if so, in what respects?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, my mandate, you know, was to monitor the zone of separation, to also monitor four border-crossing points between the Krajina and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also the protection of 13 Croat village which were in my sector. So once the Croat had re-taken, you know, the Krajina, I felt that I no longer had a mandate, and immediately afterwards beginning on the 8th, as soon as we were able, you know, to -- to move in certain area of the sector, I ordered that we start the dismantling of our observation post in order to start the repatriation process of the 4.000 plus soldiers that I had under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you engage in any activities with respect to human rights observation, monitoring, and so on, during that period?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, at least in the month of August and I think the beginning of September where the majority of my troops start to go back to their country, we accompanied the -- at least from my Canadian headquarter we accompanied the human right people in the patrol that they were doing through the area, and the same was happening from my battalion because in order for them to dismantle their observation post, they had to travel within their area, and what they were seeing, you know, they were reporting. I made clear to them in the order that I gave them that it -- our main responsibility was that the dismantling of the observation post, the repatriation of all the UN equipment, and that the monitoring of infraction to humanitarian right, that was not our first priority, but I would want them to report anything that they saw which was contrary to the normal activity or anything that was happening to humanitarian right to report it as they were doing their work or as they were travelling through their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And once in receipt of such information, did you attempt to bring that information to the attention of responsible Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I sure did. I wrote I don't know how many letter highlighting what I felt was transgression to humanitarian right or reporting activity that was taking place that were clearly, you know, against humanitarian right. Plus there was a lot of theft of UN equipment that took place during that period, which I kept reporting. My headquarter UNCRO received, also, a copy of all of letter that was sent either to General Cermak or General Gotovina. Obviously, the reason was to keep them informed and hoping, you know, also, that they could bring their influence to the Croat authority in Zagreb to stop, you know, what we were seeing as a looting, burning of house, and a lot of civilian that we found out had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you receiving information from other UN elements beyond your battalion troops?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. In my headquarter was also the command post, if can I call it like that, of the military observer, which had the responsible within Sector South. There was some civilian United Nations police, also, that were headquartered in my headquarter, and there was -- the human right people were also located within my headquarter. Every morning when I first arrived, there was a meeting at 8.30 of all of my staff, and I invited a representative of each of these organisation, and the idea of that meeting was to pass the information of what had happened in the past 24 hours, to indicate to them what we would be doing during the day, and to ask them if there was any area that they wanted us to be informed, so that information was passed, you know, on a daily basis. That was during the normal time. When the shelling started, obviously we had more frequent meeting, and as the month of August passed, we -- sometime we had two or three of those meetings during the day, depending of what was happening. They also -- excuse me. They also receive a copy of all the situation report, you know, that I was sending to my headquarter, so all of those people receive a copy of my situation report, and the majority of the letter that I wrote to either General Cermak or Gotovina I also pass a copy to Al-Alfi who was the senior humanitarian right people within my headquarter. Now, I must explain, also, that those organisation, even though were within my headquarter, they were not under my authority. I had no authority over them. I could only discuss with those people, and if there was something that they could do for me, I would ask them, you know, if they would cooperate. Overall, I think the cooperation was excellent throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I would like to turn your attention to 65 ter 1654, which can be found in tab 12 of your binder, General. General, the first page of this document indicates -- there's a reference above it to 5 August 1995. You're indicated as the releasing officer for this situation report, and it indicates enclosed -- or find enclosed a letter of protest which has been delivered to the commander of the Split Military District asking for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, as can you see, this is a -- this appears to be the letter referred to in the sitrep. It's dated 5 August 1995 sent to General Gotovina, and the subject line indicates Request for Meeting with Military Governor. And it indicates in the first line that you urgently request -- and I should mention, on the second page it is signed by you. First sentence indicates that you urgently request a meeting with the military governor of the region; indicate that a number of urgent Your Honours must be discussed, including restoration of UN freedom of movement and care of the civilian population, including displaced persons; and further indicates that there has been a significant amount of destruction and looting, and that you were not satisfied that the Croatian army is fully under control. Now, first, General, in the first line it indicates that you request a meeting with the military governor of the region. What information had you received concerning the appointment or prospective appointment of a military governor?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: If I remember well, we were in discussion with the military observer in Zadar, and I think that's where we got the first indication that what I took to be a military governor would be named, you know, to take over the responsibility of Sector South. So that's my recollection of why we used that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated in the last sentence of the first paragraph that there had been a significant amount of destruction and looting. What were you referring to in that part of the letter?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, first, what I had observed because on the 5th of August, at around 10.00, we had started to evacuate some of the wounded and some sick people from the Knin hospital, and when the last group was coming back I think at around quarter to 10.00, what they were describing to me was a bit of a confused situation, and I decided to go with the next group of -- of my four armoured personnel carrier, which I was -- we were using to move those people to go to the hospital to find out, you know, what was the situation, and when I arrived at the hospital I found out there was nobody else to be moved because the only people, the only wounded or sick that there were terminally ill, and I think my decision at that time was if I move them I might kill them, and we did not have the support required in my camp, you know, to provide -- what would be required to -- to ensure, you know, that the -- they had a chance to survive. And then I found out that the Croat army had reached the hospital because when I arrived I had seen a tank. I was not sure, you know, from whom it belonged, but eventually I saw within the hospital some Croat military. Coming back, we had pick up some ECCM people that had requested to be escorted to the camp, plus some Serb civilians that also wanted to come in my camp, and as I was coming through the town of Knin I saw some looting taking place, you know, within the main street, and I tried to talk to a lieutenant-colonel of Croat army. We had extreme difficulty because I didn't speak the language and he didn't speak French or English, but I indicate to him, you know, that those activities that was taking place was not something that should take, place. So anyhow, I saw all the looting. Plus, we were receiving information from my unit of those activities taking place, so that's where that come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how did you attempt to ensure that the letter was received by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: The same way, through the military observer at Zadar to -- through Captain Lukovic, and after that the same procedure where every time there was sending a letter that they be ensured that it was delivered, and it was confirmed that it was delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you hear back from General Gotovina in response to this letter?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: To my recollection, all the letters that I sent to General Gotovina, there never was an answer that came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you were requesting a meeting with the military governor. Did you eventually meet the person you understood to be the military governor?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yeah. The problem we were having is that as soon as the Croat forces arrived in Knin, and I was around -- around my headquarter around 11.30, we were not allowed to get out of the camp, and the first time that I met -- what I thought was the military governor was General Cermak on the 7th when Mr. Akashi came and visit in Knin. So the first time I met with Mr. Akashi, General Cermak, myself, and there may have been other people in my -- in my office at my headquarter, then I asked at that time General Cermak, you know, to have a meeting because he presented to my recollection himself as the -- in the translation it was to me the military governor who was responsible of the Knin region. And I asked that we had a meeting that day, which did occur, you know, sometime late in the afternoon after the departure of Mr. Akashi. And at that particular meeting I was there; Mr. Al-Alfi was responsible for the Human Rights Action Team, and there may have been other people, but at least Mr. Al-Alfi was there. And every time that I met with General Cermak, Mr. Al-Alfi or his representative was there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let me ask you to turn to tab 14 of your binder. That would be 65 ter 3252.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, if you'll look at paragraph 8 -- first of all, I should have drawn your attention, although you can see that on your copy, to the date of this sitrep, which is 8 August 1995 at 0730. Paragraph 8 is a entitled "Report of Meeting, Commander Sector South/Military Governor Region." It indicates commander Sector South, yourself, met with General Cermak in the military governor headquarters (former ARSK headquarters) at 1800 hours, 7 August, to discuss items of mutual interest. And does this reflect the meeting with General Cermak that took place after you met him during the course of the meeting with Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, it indicates that you met in the former ARSK headquarters. I believe you indicated in your 2008 statement at paragraph 12 that you saw little, if any, damage to the ARSK Ministry of Defence on August 4th. What -- was that the same building that you're referring to in this sitrep where you met General Cermak on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I believe that is, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you see any significant signs of damage to that building when you met General Cermak on that date?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Not that I remember, and on the 4th, I went twice to that same building, and I don't remember seeing any damage to that particular building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we turn to the next page, and at -- to the last paragraph in particular, there's an indication at the beginning of that paragraph about a question on special measures to ensure the safety of populations especially at night. What was the concern about the safety of the populations especially at night? Which population? Safety from whom?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, throughout this sitrep in a manner consistent with what you indicated before, you refer to General Cermak as the military governor. Did you also refer to him as a military governor in correspondence that you sent to him?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Every letter that I sent to him was addressed to the military governor of Knin, and there was never any return letter that he sent me indicating that I should not address him like that or the meeting that I had with him where he would indicate to me that he was not the military governor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of your discussions with him, and in particular those during which you were bringing to his attention violations of human rights and demanding action, did he indicate to you that he was not the appropriate person to be bringing these complaints to or that he was not the -- the military governor of the area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that every time we brought him something, you know, he -- sometime he was denying, you know, that this was happening, but he never indicate -- or he would say, I would look into the matters, you know, and I will take care of it. He never indicate to me that he was not responsible for the area where those problem were arising from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as far as you're concerned, did you make it apparent to him during the course of your meetings that you considered him to be the person responsible for the area and from whom you expected action?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And I remember that I had met the General Gotovina, I think, on the 6th of August where he told me at that meeting that now I had to deal with General Cermak, as he was the individual responsible for the Knin region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look next at your initial meeting with General Gotovina following Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn, please, to 65 ter 2771. And the next page, please. I'm sorry, if we could stay on that page just a moment and then -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, General, I simply wanted to indicate the date of this particular document. It's a sitrep of 8 August 1995 at 2030 hours as indicated in the date/time section of the document, and it is indicated in the subject line below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn quickly to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The initial portion of the document reflects a commander's assessment. I take it that's your assessment, General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you indicate that you met that day with both Colonel General Gotovina and the military governor of Knin General Cermak, and you go on to describe some aspects of those meetings. We'll turn to a report of that meeting -- of those meetings in just a moment. You -- and the daily sitrep also indicates at paragraph (c) all units report looting as a general activity for HV soldiers. Random shooting of livestock and wanton destruction of farms and houses is observed wherever we are allowed to travel. The HV seem determined to clean up the evidence of their military tactics in taking the Krajina. The shell holes in the road Knin-Drnis that were observed this morning were patched by this afternoon. Now, let me turn your attention, General, to the third page of this document, which is headed -- which has a portion headed Report Of Meeting Commander Sector South and Commander Military District South and indicates that Colonel General Gotovina invited commander Sector South to the Knin fortress for a meeting at 0920. Now, General, this meeting is addressed at paragraph 7 of your 2008 statement in which you state that although it is not reflected in the sitrep, you recall complaining to General Gotovina about the lack of discipline of his troops and that they were looting and burning in the town. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you earlier noted that General Gotovina in the first meeting you had with him after Operation Storm had directed you to General Cermak. There's a reference, it seems, to that in the last sentence of the first paragraph. And does that reflect what you were mentioning a moment earlier about being referred to General Cermak, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But I don't think he used the term "military governor." It's us in all our correspondence that that's the interpretation that I had when I had first met with General Cermak, so we kept using the term "military governor," but I don't recall that General Gotovina used that term himself. What he portrayed to me was that General Cermak was in charge of the Knin region, and any problem that I had I would have to go to General Cermak to settle that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And that would include the problems you raised with him at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you meet with General -- you did meet with General Cermak later that day, is that right, and that is reflected in paragraph B?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be indicated in the section that General -- Colonel - it says here Colonel, actually - Cermak came to HQ Sector South at 1300 to meet first with you and then to meet with a committee of IVPs; that would be internally displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after your discussion with General Gotovina, did you in fact bring, again, your concern over the crimes that had been reported to you to the attention of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's reflected at least in part in paragraph 2: Commander Sector South expressed concern over reports of organised looting on the road between Knin and Drnis and includes livestock being loaded into trucks and removed, the complete contents of houses being packed up in trucks under the supervision of civil police. And the military governor stated that this was possible due to the immensity of the operation he was conducting. General, do you recall anything further about that discussion with General Cermak concerning your concerns about the crimes that were taking place and his anticipated response to that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, you know, that particular meeting, except that at every meeting that I had with him, you know, those points were raised. So for that particular one, no, because the biggest problem I had obviously was the complaint, you know, of the fact that the looting and the burning because once in a while a house, a fire would start, you know. From what we were observing in Knin, there was firing in the air once in a while, and the report that we were receiving from our unit was that similar activity was taking place. My biggest problem was that I could not get out of the -- my headquarter at that particular time in order, you know, to go and find out exactly what was happening, nor any other people that was within my compound, except the only individual that was allowed to go out was Captain Hill who was the military police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was it you learned from Captain Hill after he went out?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, he went out, and I had asked him, you know, to have a look about the extent of the damage and what was taking place, you know, within Knin, and he came back and he reported to me in the afternoon, I think, around 4.00 that he had seen extensive damage, that he had seen looting. He had went to the apartment that I had occupied with my driver, cook, and this had been vandalized and, you know, the majority of the stuff that we had had been stolen. So that's what he reported to me when he came back. I think it was on the 6th in the afternoon. The 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. General, I'm going to ask you some questions about some of those aspects that you referred to, your dealings with General Cermak concerning restriction of movement, various human rights violations. You also mentioned earlier the looting or theft of UN property as well. But I also want, first, to direct your attention to something else you mention. That was the displaced persons in the camp. And can you tell the Court something about the discussions that took place with General Cermak concerning the disposition or fate of the displaced persons who had been taken into UNCRO Sector South headquarters or who were being -- or who were in other detention or collection facilities in Knin.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, this went on over numbers of discussion. Initially, I think the number we had on the 6th was around 700 IDP in the camp, and the majority of them were Serb. We also had, I think, 40 and 50 Croat Serbs, you know, the Croat from the Krajina that was also in the compound, and the -- at that particular meeting General Cermak wanted to meet, and he met with the IDP, and obviously I do not understand their conversation, but what he told me is that he wanted to advise them that they could go back to the area where they come from and they would be provided within the unit area, if I remember well, within the Canadian battalion headquarter, I think they were up to 30 Serb that took refuge in their camp. There was 20 to 25 with the Czech battalion area, and there were a few with the Kenyan battalion and the Jordanian battalion. Eventually, we came to an agreement with General Cermak that all of these people were allowed to be moved within my camp. There came a period of time, I think, around the third week of August where there was still some more of those displaced people, but I had passed my capacity within my camp. I already had problem where it's a camp that was designed for about 350 people, and we were hovering around 1.800 to 2.000. We were able to provide only two meals a day because even though I had asked some field kitchen from the Canadian battalion, the time it took us to feed all of those people, we begin at 7.00 and we finish at around 12.30, and we begin the supper around 3.00 to finish around 7.30. So we discuss with Mr. Al-Alfi and General Cermak the possibility that if there was other people that were displaced people that he should house them, which happened. There's a facility that was found in Knin where I think 4 to 500 of those people were placed, and the day that finally it was decided that they could go back -- or not go back but go to Serbia they were all put together, and that's why that number, you know, which confused me initially when I was talking about the thousands was 1.184 that left Knin for Serbia, I think, on the 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention quickly to 65 ter 4949. That's in tab 31 of your binder. And that's a sitrep dated the 21st of August at 2030 hours and reflects -- I'm sorry, moving too fast. Okay. If we could turn to page 2, please. Okay. As we see from page 2, that reflects a meeting between -- involving you, the humanitarian and political coordinator, and the military governor, General Cermak, concerning the -- the departure of displaced persons. And it refers in that second paragraph to a list of people who wished to leave Croatia from the camp, 687 persons out of a total population of approximately 731, and also indicates in the third paragraph that General Cermak indicated he had a list of persons under suspicion of war crimes. General, was -- and I'm sorry. If we turn the page once more. And it indicates that General Cermak should be able to provide a list of those persons by the next day and that once that list was provided there would be no further checks by the Croatian authorities. First of all, let me ask you a couple of questions about this, General Forand. First, do you know or did you have contact with the displaced person that allowed you to -- gave you insight into why 687 persons out of that 731 wished to leave rather than return to their homes in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, I was talking once in a while with the IDP committee, and their indication was they did not want to stay, you know, because they didn't feel that their security would be guaranteed. In that sitrep, because at that time I was only a conduit because the decision, you know, was out of my hand. It was at the UNCRO level and at the UNPROFOR level about the situation regarding the displaced people. But what was discussed at that stage was the possibility that we would keep those people that they had identified as war criminal within the camp and leave the other IDP the possibility, you know, to return to Serbia immediately, and that's the essence of the discussion that was taking place. The other thing as I have mentioned earlier is that I did not want to accept any more additional IDP in the camp because I could not provide for them, and we discussed the possibility that General Cermak found a place, if there was more of those people that he should accommodate them. You will see later on that we thought we had a deal at one point that we could send those that had not been identified as war criminals back to Serbia, but at the end of the month it was vetoed and nothing came out of it, and only when alias agreed upon, I think 34 or 35 were identified with sufficient proof that the UN said, okay, those people can be given to the Croat authority, where the rest of the IDP allowed to go back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Forand, we will have a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, we had earlier looked at the sitrep from August 8th at 2030 - that is 65 ter 2771 - which reflected the meetings that took place on that date. There was -- that document reflected that reference to the restrictions of movement you had talked about earlier in the paragraph B1 saying, he, meaning General Cermak, began by indicating that as soon as he returned to his HQ he would give orders that UN elements would be allowed to travel freely within Knin and to Drnis-something --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsellor. Can we just bring that up on the screen, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. And it's 2771.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the second page, please. Sorry, the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as indicated, I was reading from B1. That's the second paragraph from the bottom. And just to conclude, after mentioning that the portion where it said General Cermak would give orders that UN elements be allowed to travel freely within Knin and to Drnis. "Something he had been prevented from doing until now due to the pressure of his schedule." General, if we could next turn to tab -- excuse me, to 65 ter 4919, and that's tab 16 of your binder, General. And I'm going to want to ask you when you see that document whether that's the -- whether that's the order to travel freely that was referred to in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the one, except where limited in Knin and Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, if I could ask you turn next, then, to 65 ter 3253. That's a sitrep of 9 August at 2030. And if we could turn to the next page, please, under Commander's Assessment. Sorry, perhaps I read the wrong number. I'm looking for 65 ter 3253. Have I got the wrong page? Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We just looked, General Forand, at the document dated August 8th concerning movement in Knin and Drnis. This sitrep on the 9th reflects a meeting that day with General Cermak and further discussion about freedom of movement. And if you look in particular at paragraph (c), it indicates that restrictions on freedom of movement continue, particularly affecting the Knin area, resupply for units, and liaison between units and HQ SS. General Cermak claims total authority over the area of Sector South and grants freedom of movement. HV units in CanBat 1 AOR, in particular Benkovac, deny General Cermak's authority and even his existence. Confusion in HV ranks has worn thin as a reason for continued ROM. I take it that's restrictions of movement?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The evidence of methodical and continuous destruction that is observed whenever we can travel suggests the real reason. General Forand, did you raise with General Cermak on August 9th your concerns about the limitations on movement notwithstanding the document that had been issued on August 8th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. What is in this sitrep is a -- a sort of a resume, you know, the discussion that took place with him. Every time that I met with General Cermak, Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk who was my Senior Liaison Officer was with me, and he was the one taking the notes, and when we come back and preparing the situation report for the day, we used this note, you know, in order to compile the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to look next at 65 ter 553 -- no, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, General. Your Honours, 65 ter 553.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, for your information, it's at tab 22 of your binder, but I think you will see it on the screen in a moment. This is directed to your attention. It's a document dated August 11th from General Cermak to you referencing your letter of August 10th, 1995, concerning freedom of movement. And it refers in the line below the reference line to the agreement between the Republic of Croatia government and UNCRO of 6 August 1995. And, General, is this a document -- first of all, did you receive this document, and are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it, and I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is this a document that purported to expand the freedom of movement that had been provided on August 8th to all of the sector?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, and a copy of that was made and sent to all my units and also was provided to the -- the UNMO that were in the headquarter, the UN Civilian Police and the Human Rights Action Team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you indicated at page 18 of your -- of exhibit number 331 - that's your 1997 statement; that would be page 10 of the B/C/S - that full freedom of movement did not happen for about ten days after Knin was taken. Can you tell us whether or not the receipt of this document resulted in free access by UNCRO and other elements of the UN into areas within the sector that -- where they wanted to check on conditions?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No. There's all kind of documented situation report that highlights that the freedom of movement was restricted in many area and in many days, and this paper which was supposed to allow us that freedom of movement did not guarantee it. We -- it was problem, you know, throughout the sector for numerous days, and it went on, as far as I can remember, almost to the -- the end of the August and even certain time in September where there were reported by HRAT and some UNMO and some of my military within the unit that their movement were restricted, which was in contradiction to the reference that is done in that letter to Article 4 and 5 of the deal that was made between the agreement between the government of the Republic of Croatia and United Nations peace force, UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you focus in a moment on some particular exchanges involving restrictions of movement in particular documents, but before I do I wanted to quickly take up one other issue you mentioned, and that was the theft of UN equipment, and -- since you raised it. And if I could ask you turn your attention next to 65 ter 460. General, that's at tab 23 of your binder while we're waiting for it to come up. This is a document dated August 11th, 1995. It is a protest to General Cermak, theft of engineer equipment. And in the first paragraph, it references a meeting the previous day and General Cermak's request for more precise information on the engineer equipment taken from a particular area. And if we go -- without going into the details of the particular equipment which can be found in the document, Caterpillar road grader, mine roller, et cetera, which you indicate at the bottom of the first page has an approximate value of 1 million dollars, if we could simply turn to the last paragraph of the document in which you ask General Cermak to use his considerable influence to ensure the return of the engineer plant taken from the UN by HV elements as well as the additional vehicles mentioned above and the three UN vehicles stolen from the garage in Knin while under repair as mentioned in my earlier letter on this subject. General, do you know what actions were taken in response to this request, and was the -- was your request fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: To my recollection, no, it was not fulfilled, and there are similar letters like that where other UN equipment had been stolen, and I don't remember that it was ever returned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can just turn very quickly to 65 ter 462.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a letter dated August 19th, 1995 from you to General Cermak referencing your earlier letter of 11 August and indicating where you believed the armoured Caterpillar dozer is located and the fact that a mixed team of UN and military police were denied access to that location and requesting an escort. Is that one of the follow-up letters you referred to, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And turn next to 65 ter 459. It's another letter of 19 August 1995 from you to General Cermak protesting the theft of UN vehicles and equipment, listing a number of UN vehicles - ten, I believe - and noting below the list of those vehicles that the ones marked with a asterisk were observed being driven in Knin by HV soldiers on August 10th. Is that another one of the documents referred to, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one more in that series. 65 ter 1795, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is also a letter of August 19th, 1995, from you to General Cermak, again, regarding the theft of UN equipment and accommodation. And this refers to, among other things, ISO accommodation containers, which were observed being placed onto flat-bed trucks by men wearing HV uniforms who were armed. Can you tell us quickly what an ISO accommodation container is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: It what we used to replace our tent. It was used to house military soldier in order to sleep in. It was about 25 feet by 12 feet, if I remember well, the dimension. So it's a fairly big -- fairly big container.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And the first part of your answer says it was used to replace our tank, it says. I didn't understand what that meant. You can see the answer on the transcript in front of you, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it tank, or is it tent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tent. Yeah, not tanks. We didn't have no tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you earlier indicated that General Gotovina on August 8th had referred you to General Cermak to deal with the kinds of problems you raised with him on that occasion. Notwithstanding that indication, did you finally turn to General Gotovina in connection with this matter of the attempt to recover the stolen UN property?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. There came a point because every time I was meeting with General Cermak with Mr. Al-Alfi, it was very sociable, you know, and he was telling us that it would taking care of the -- they would take care of the problem, but nothing was ever settled. There was still some burning that was taking place, some looting, some equipment, UN equipment that was stolen, so I decided because of a lot of the activity where it was taking place they were people dressed as HV soldier that I decided that I would go to General Gotovina and ensure that he was aware, you know, that certain of those activity involve military personnel from the HV and hopefully, you know, that he would be able to do something about it. So that's the reason why I think I sent him two letter on that particular subject highlighting the stolen equipment, the looting and burning where some HV soldier were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to 65 ter 1840, please. This is letter dated 26 -- oops. Yeah. First of all, this is a sitrep of 26 August of 2100, which attaches an enclosed letter, which was being sent to General Gotovina. That's found at the next page -- and I won't skip around, but we'll -- we can look at the last page in a moment, but it's a letter from you or signed by you, General, to General Gotovina on August 26th. At the beginning of the document, it references the meeting of August 8th, and you indicate that indeed you are working with General Cermak. And then the letter goes on to address the issue of both hostile acts carried out by HV against UN peacekeepers, and the -- on the second page, and the issue of UN equipment as seen in the second full paragraph. And finally in the last paragraph of that page, it indicates as a minor matter, a request for some assistance in putting together a historical appreciation, it's called here, which I take it is some form of presentation concerning Operation Storm. General, is this the letter that you sent to General Gotovina through the normal channels, and did you receive any response?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I did not receive any response, but I must also retract what I said because I thought in that letter, I -- what I had talk about looting and burning, which is not the case. I'm referring to the conduct of military soldier and the fact, you know, that UN equipment has been stolen and we would like to have it back, but nowhere do I mention the looting and burning that was still taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let me ask you a question about that. You were in the area for that period of time. Based on what you saw when you toured the sector, based on your conversations with other people who were in the sector, was it possible to be within the sector at any time and not know about the looting and burning?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, it would have been extremely difficult because as is indicated in all the situation report, you know, once we were allowed to move within the sector, almost on a daily basis they are report of looting, burning, or killing of an animals, plus once in a while, you know, people that had been murdered. All the letter that I have sent to General Cermak indicate, you know, that those problems were continuously arriving and the fact that every time that we were meeting with General Cermak not only I but Mr. Al-Alfi was also indicating to him that looting and burning were taking place in addition to some murder that were committed, so I find it almost impossible, you know, that they would not be aware. Plus, there was our public affair officer that was also doing quite a lot of writing about this particular subject, Mr. Alun Roberts, who it is pretty hard to understand if it was not known, you know, at all level that those activity were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, General, I may return to one aspect of the theft of UN equipment a bit later, but I'd like to turn now to two of the issues you mentioned before, and that is the observation -- the awareness of the crimes, human rights violations you spoke of and the restrictions of movement that were simultaneously taking place. Now, you begin in your statement in 1996 at page 10, and it's page 9 of the B/C/S. You indicated that from the moment the war ended, the systematic looting of villages and towns, the burning of buildings and crops, and the wanton killing or wholesale theft of livestock began. You've indicated some of what you saw at the early stages, and I'd like to move through at least some of the documents in connection with the -- your exchanges with General Cermak in particular but also General Gotovina about those issues. So, first -- well, let me ask you -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
