utterances.text: Let's just turn, first, then, please, to 65 ter 3256.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, General, I believe you had indicated in your testimony earlier about the looting that had taken place in Knin in the -- immediately after the HV entered. This is a letter dated August 9th, 1995, from you to General Cermak concerning various issues of importance. And if we could turn to the -- look at the last paragraph, indicating that -- your comment to General Cermak that you would also appreciate greater control of his personnel after -- and then we just read this: "After cleaning up their accommodation yesterday, many of my personnel returned to their apartments to find that they had again been broken into and some additional contents removed. This type of lawlessness is doing little to inspire confidence in my staff who would like to again take up residence in Knin and contribution to the normalisation of life." So these reflect events that took place after the initial looting that you had referred to earlier, General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yeah because the looting I saw was on the 5th of August when I was returning from the hospital and also the looting that I saw taking place in front of my headquarter were -- when we were surrounded. Some of the IDP had left their vehicle outside of the gate because obviously there was no place in my compound, and we saw some HV troops, you know, looting the content of those vehicle. That's the extent of the looting I saw, and that letter refer before I went outside of the camp, you know, which was on the 12th when I went to Donji Lapac. This refer to once we had received the permission to get out of the camp. There was a lot of people, UN civilian people some military observers on UN police that had location, they were staying within the Knin town, so they went back to their apartment, and they found out that it had been looted. According to that, I don't exactly remember how many of them, you know, it happened. They cleaned up, and when they went back the next day, you know, some looting again had taken place. That's why that paragraph was inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as UNCRO and other UN elements began to move around the sector, I think you indicated they began to discover more evidence of looting and burning. I'd like to you turn to 65 ter 576, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking quickly at the paragraph marked General Situation, which indicates -- it refers to the freedom of movement letter received from General Cermak and some continuing problems in that regard. Also refers to smoke, fires continuing to mark the landscape of the Krajina and random shots and explosions heard continuously in all areas. And finally, the last paragraph: Reports are being received that the area leading to and surrounding Donji Lapac has been the scene of appalling ethnic cleansing; the SC, sector commander will tour the area tomorrow. And that's the tour -- the trip to Donji Lapac you referred to just a moment ago, General. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was done on the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. And at the bottom of this page, it also indicates that two letters of protest were delivered to General Cermak. One was on the occupation of the CanBat camp at Civljane, and the second on the apparent systematic destruction of civilian and UN properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could move through two more pages of the document, please. And one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a letter dated August 11th, 1995, to General Cermak from you, indicating at the beginning of the document: "During our meeting yesterday, both Mr. Paavo Pitcanen and I brought to your attention information gathered by UN sources concerning the widespread and systematic looting and destruction of property, crops, and livestock. Since that meeting, additional reports of such needless destruction in the area between Knin and Pakovo Selo and along the former Zone of Separation have reached me. Recalling your statements during yesterday's meeting concerning your honest efforts to control the situation, I again protest these activities and ask to redouble your efforts to prevent the organised destruction and theft of property." So General, this document is one of the letters of -- one of the protests you brought to General Cermak's attention concerning what was happening in the sector?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether the crimes that you brought to his attention continued or not?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, it continued because as you will see later on, you know, the similar letter that was sent to him and discussion during our meeting that took place concerning those particular subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that regard, General, I'd like you to turn next to two documents, please, and those will be 65 ter 2467 and then a document already in evidence, D151. So let me ask to you look at those in order. First, 2467. This is a sitrep dated 24 August 1995 at 2030 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the third page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It indicates at the top a meeting at 1330 hours between you, commander Sector South, the political and humanitarian affairs coordinator, and General Cermak. And it first discusses the issue of the displaced persons that you had earlier mentioned and the impossibility of allowing any displaced persons to depart for Serbia until 62 persons accused of war crimes were handed over. And then in paragraph 6, it indicates that General Cermak was then reminded of the continuing burning and looting of homes taking place in the Sector South area, and he was asked to stop such acts. General Cermak initially responded by attributing such acts to bandits in army uniforms but then admitted that his area of responsibility is vast and it is difficult to exert control everywhere. He said he sincerely regretted such acts which were contrary to the policy of the government of Croatia. Before I ask you about that, I also wanted you to look at D151. You indicated, General, that Mr. Al-Alfi accompanied you to many of these meetings and the sitrep of August 24th indicates that he was present there. And is it correct that General Al-Alfi took his own notes of these meetings and produced his own record of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when those were sent out, were they sent to you, as well, and you sent yours to him?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed in -- he received also a copy of my own sitrep, and as far as I can recall he attended the great majority of the meeting that I had with General Cermak. If he was not there, he was represented by one of his personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, again, this refers to the meeting at 1330 hours of August 24th. Indicates the initial discussion about the impossibilities of departure of the displaced persons until the handover of the 62 suspected or accused persons. And then in the final paragraph, paragraph 5 indicates the following: "We brought the continuation of burning houses and looting in the area to the attention of General Cermak and asked him to stop such acts. He accepted this fact, regarding the continuation of such incidents and attributed them to 'persons who entered the area wearing HV uniforms and to civilians taking revenge.' He also attribute the such acts to ongoing efforts by the Croatian army 'who are still clearing the terrain and capturing the rebels.' General Cermak made it clear that in his opinion the area is very vast and he would be lying if he told us nothing of this sort would continue to happen, but he informed us that he has already issued strict orders to the civilian and military personnel to stop such acts." General, are these to the best of your recollection accurate accounts of yet another occasion on which you brought to General Cermak's attention the ongoing crimes and asked him to see that they were curtailed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. And as you can see, Mr. Al-Alfi used different word but the meaning is similar to what was included in my situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated earlier there were occasions on which -- I think you indicated earlier that the meetings were cordial but there were various responses. Sometimes General Cermak would indicate he would deal with it, and do you recall other occasions on which General Cermak indicated that he would issue orders to civilian and military personnel to stop the ongoing crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I recall a couple of occasion where he stated that he would look into it and take care of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask one question between. Mr. Tieger used a couple of times now and we also find it in this report by Mr. Al-Alfi the expression "to stop the ongoing crimes." Now, from my understanding of the English language, it could mean two things. If I want you to stop certain things, then it could be that I ask you to stop doing that. There's another way of stopping, that is, stopping that other people are doing that. Since Mr. Tieger just read orders would be issued to stop the ongoing crimes, did you understand this to be that they had to stop doing these things or that they had to stop others doing these kind of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood that they had to stop doing these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not to stop others from doing it but not to commit such acts any further --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I thought -- I understood that it was his own people, you know, from stopping doing those type of activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next to -- I'd like to turn next to a meeting on the 29th of August, and again, I'm going to ask you to look at a number of accounts of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, first, if we could turn to 65 ter 3075. This is a sitrep or a situation report from August 29th at 2030 hours. And if we could turn to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, General. That would be -- that's tab 36. My apologies. And the second page, it refers to a meeting apparently at 1230 hours, again, involving you, Mr. Al-Alfi, and General Cermak, and, again, involving issues related to displaced persons and also in this case to former members of the ARSK; and indicates among other things that Croatian authorities would offer alternatives to HQ Sector South camp, that UN agencies will not encourage persons who leave their villages and come to those shelters, and in the next paragraph a reference to what to do about former members of the ARSK wishing to surrender and how to do that, involving UN making contact with Croatian authorities, including General Cermak. If I could ask you to look next at 65 ter 4162, and that is found in tab 37 of your binder. And this is Mr. Al-Alfi's report on the meeting of that date with General Cermak and yourself. Again, identifies a number of those same issues. Beginning -- it begins with the reiteration to General Cermak of the need for increasing the security guarantees in the villages; and it continues on the second page addressing a number of the issues mentioned earlier and also asking General Cermak to use his good offices in connection with the provision of ten houses for UNCRO personnel who lost their accommodation in Knin; an inquiry about the process of investigation in the case of what happened in Grubori where a number of civilians were killed and houses burnt; and an indication by General Cermak that tomorrow, 30 August, he will identify areas restricted to UNCRO starting 31st August 1995 because those areas will witness major cleaning operations by the Croatian army. And, finally, General, one more record of that meeting. This is 65 ter 3069 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you allow me one question in between. One of these lines just read to you is that ten houses were needed for UNCRO personnel who lost their accommodation. Could you -- have you any recollection on how they lost their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's those apartment that were looted, Your Honour, and it could not be refurbish sufficiently, you know, for them to be housed, so we had asked because I had a problem of lodging within my camp if it would be possible to have a certain number of house, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at 65 ter 3069, again, a record of the meeting from -- of August 29th, 1995, this time from Croatian authorities involving you and Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's further discussion about the ARSK soldiers and how they should -- not further discussion but there's reflection of that discussion about the ARSK soldiers. A further discussion about the stolen UN vehicles, some of them as Mr. Al-Alfi says, "currently being driven around Knin by the HV. The last time I saw one was two days ago." And that refers back to the ongoing issue we had mentioned before and General Cermak's response, "I have a list. I submitted it to the civilian and military police. This is very embarrassing for me, but the answer is still negative. I will repeat my orders." And finally on the last page, the request for information about Grubori as mentioned in both the previous documents and the indication at the bottom of the page about the planning for a mop-up operation and the blocking of roads, about which the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, but could we just go to the next page. I mean, I appreciate the speed, but I prefer to exactly what you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can see there, the -- it was the reference to Grubori on the bottom of the previous page. Cermak's response ... and that our units involved in clearing up the territory reported that three renegades and two civilians had been killed, several cattle sheds set on fire while some rebels had fled. And then at the bottom, the reference to an upcoming mop-up operation, large-scale mop-up operation and the blocking of roads. Now, General Forand, first of all we see again a reference to the issue of the stolen UN vehicles and another indication of General Cermak indicating that he will issue orders to see that's addressed. Was this another occasion on which General Cermak assured you that the problems you brought to his attention -- that he would deal with the problems you brought to his attention and would issue orders to see that they were resolved?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom, at the -- and indicated that there was a reference to those documents to an anticipated restriction of movement on -- by HV forces on the UN. Do you recall whether you protested this restriction of movement?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, I don't recall protesting at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before we move to any other document, could you pay specific attention to some issues of translation of this document. I was -- my attention was triggered by the fact that the minuted start with General Ivan probably Cermak, which seems to be an interpretation rather -- and I mean, interpretation can mean two things. The original doesn't say Ivan; it says I, and then says Cerkak, and then apparently the person who translated this document has started to figure out who that might be and then gave his own opinion about that, which of course is not what we expect to be translation. At the same time, I ask the Defence, it looks as this is not -- this is not an illogical conclusion, if there's any party who would consider that at least the minutes are referring to any other person than a General Cermak, then I'd like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's no issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- Your Honour. The accuracy -- I see it's a draft as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that is a problem that we all face with a number of these documents, and that is out of our hands. We're powerless to rectify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there is no issue about it. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm informed by Mr. Misetic one particular version, and if we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The English translation as it pertains to the Croatian, and apparently according to the -- Mr. Misetic, in this particular document, Mr. Al-Alfi is looking for accommodations to move into town, which is certainly a tad bit different than what the witness testified about replacing damaged houses. I don't know if there some discrepancy in the translation or in the original, but I bring that to your attention, Your Honour, because Mr. Misetic said there appeared to be some discrepancy between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Discrepancy is one; an issue of translation is, of course, another matter. There may be discrepancy between what the witness testifies and what we find in this document, which is of a different nature than any inaccuracy in the translation. If there would be any similar concern about the translation, I invite Mr. Misetic to bring this to the attention of Mr. Tieger so that can he specifically draw the attention when this draft translation will be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we'll certainly -- in light of -- I think I understand it from the comments just made, but if there is any question I'll certainly consult with Mr. Misetic about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're invited to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think, Your Honour, if I could ... If we could turn next to 65 ter 3544, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a letter dated 30 August 1995 from you to General Cermak. That's the day after the meeting and indicates as follows. I wish to advise you that following consultation with UNCRO in Zagreb and with reference to the 6 August agreement, I am unable to accept any unilateral restriction of movement imposed by your office in the area of my command. And then specifically cites in the next paragraph the questions that have been raised in recent weeks in the sector, including the events in Grubori on 26th August, and the view that such restrictions as intended are intended to prevent UNCRO from fully exercising its agreed task to monitor human rights and the observance of international obligations. General, was this a response to the -- do you recall this as a response to the indications that there be further restrictions of movement -- that is, the indications on August 29th there would be further restrictions of movement?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but as I mentioned, I didn't raise it with General Cermak at the 29th meeting, but when I went back to my headquarter I phoned my headquarter and asked for clarification as to the agreement that had been made between Mr. Akashi and the Croatian government, and the advice I receive was that they were not allowed to limit our movement. It was to be done in consultation with me, but it seems from their interpretation that I had the last word if we would be going or not. And what General Cermak had alluded on the previous day that they would be some operation within a portion of my area where we would not be allowed to move at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe there was a response that same day. Let me direct your attention to 65 ter 3531. This is a letter from General Cermak to you on the same date, indicating that -- in reply to your letter that General Cermak wishes to inform you that his intention was not to restrict the movement -- the freedom of movement of UNCRO officers but draw your attention to the danger your officers might be exposed to should they happen to be moving through the area where we intend to start a large-scale mopping-up operations tomorrow to clear the territory of defeated enemy troops. Indicates at the bottom that there is an enclosed map and the operation will go on. And in the sentence above that their intention was to seal -- that is, General Cermak indicated "our intention was to seal off the area in order to ensure the personal safety of your officers as well as members of other international organisations." General, can you -- did this letter mean that you would -- you and the UN would have freedom of movement through the sector or would be restricted from entering the areas which were sealed off by Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it could be read two way. One way it allowed us to go wherever we want; the second one, because it refers to the map which were to show us the area where we would not be allowed. It could be a way of indicating that with that map this is the area where we will conduct operation, and you will not be allowed to go. It's not clear, you know, in that letter. That's why I say it could go both ways. And I don't remember, you know, what we did following the receipt of that letter, if we went anyhow. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can look at some further documents to see how -- to see what followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could look next at -- first at 65 ter 2559.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will come up on your screen, General, but, sorry, it is at tab 41 of your binder. This is a sitrep dated 31 August at 2030 hours. If you turn to the second page, it's the commander's assessment. It indicates the following: "Burning of houses and villages continues in a steady and methodical manner. Every day brings incidents or stories of atrocities against people and property, including murder and the wholesale destruction of livestock. The numbers of police and militaries whose presence dominates everything in the Krajina makes it very difficult to believe that these activities are occurring without at least the tacit approval of the authorities. More believable are the explanations from low-ranking Croatian soldiers, often returned from other countries that he have been promised virgin land for homesteading in the Krajina after the war is won." And in paragraph (b), it refers to the tightening, again, of restrictions of movements of UN personnel, military, UNMOs, ECMM and states "temporary," in quotes, "restrictions due to Serbian terrorist fighting are the new line, although coincidentally, these areas are the same ones that have been subject to press coverage of atrocities or are areas that suddenly burst into flame. An example is the area surrounding Donji Lapac yesterday. See protest." Indicates in the last paragraph, paragraph (c), that you have been advised by General Cermak that extensive clearing operations will take place, and that is being protested. And in that -- General, is that your assessment of the situation at the end of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a quick look at a document already in evidence, D144. That's found at tab 42. This is a letter dated 31 August 1995 from you to General Cermak, and the subject line is Protest, Restriction of Movement, Continuation Of Burnings, and it advises in the first paragraph that further to your letter protesting the restriction of movement along the road to Donji Lapac at the major intersection near Otric: "I must inform that the human rights monitoring team later observed heavy smoke rising from the forest in the restricted area. The same team also observed five houses burning near Gracac." Then you go on to say, and I raise this in particular, General, because we'll see a response to that in a moment: "These restrictions of movement combined with unexplained burnings leave many unanswered questions. I do not understand how those under your command are able to control so effectively all movement and at the same time almost one month after hostilities so many houses continue to be burned, driving poor and destitute persons homeless from their land in contravention of the policy of the government of Croatia. It is requested that you invest the resources necessary to control such acts of lawlessness within your area of responsibility. "I also request that you stop restricting the movement of UN elements. If you are sincere about stopping the wanton destruction of property, then I urge you to welcome the independent surveillance of UN teams as a valuable tool in countering this banditry." General, what did you hope to achieve by sending this letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, whenever you read would you keep in mind that usually speed goes up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, did this letter have the intended effect of ensuring the end of restrictions of movement of UN elements and the end of the crimes that you were pointing out?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: If it had -- what's your question? If it did stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, I don't think it did stop because you will see later on, you know, that the same thing is happening. In mine, like in all the aim of the previous letter, was to advise him that those thing were taking place, and I felt that it was his responsibility because he had told me that he was responsible for the region of Knin, which encompassed my area of responsibility that those activities should cease because it was not according to humanitarian right, you know, so there was a reason for all those letter and all those meeting where we repeated most of the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to turn, then, to 65 ter 4750. And, General, this is a sitrep from the 3rd of September, 1995, at 1515 hours. And in connection with what you've just indicated to the Court, it states as follows: "In spite of the strenuous efforts to identify and stem human rights violations committed in the aftermath of OP Storm, references A and B the most recent, the burning, looting, and pillaging of the homes and farms of impoverished Serbs continues in Sector South. Despite the official statement of the Croatian government urging Serbs to remain in their villages, the military governor of Knin is either unable or unwilling to put an end to the widespread and systematic destruction of the only means of subsistence available to these vulnerable and innocent victims of war. This is criminal. Is there nothing which can be done?" And then in the last paragraph, you urge your headquarters to pursue all means available to stop the abuse of human rights in the sector. Now, General, you also received a response from General Cermak on that date to your letter of 31 August. I want to show that you document and ask you if this situation report was sent before or after you received that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page. This is a -- I don't know how the Court wants to resolve this, Your Honour. This is actually D145, this particular page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a letter, General Forand, from General Cermak to you regarding your letter of 31 August and your letter of 1 September. It's a reply to the protest about alleged restriction of movement. And it provides as follows, in part: "In the same letter, you state that 'restriction of movement combined with unexplainable burning of houses leave many questions unanswered.' I am astonished at your statements about persecution of the poor and the miserable from their land, which I consider are strong words and ungrounded accusations. "I ask you to give evidence of at least one case of driving people out of their homes and burning their houses. Furthermore, we ask you kindly to be careful your letters do not contain any insinuations without proofs. I am ready to go with you to prove the truth in any case at any time." First question, General: Do you recall whether you had this response from General Cermak to your 31 August letter before you sent the sitrep of September 3rd?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I don't remember, but my sitrep of the 3rd at 1515 does not allude to that letter, and to me it has no bearing. You know, based on that letter, it's a constatation [sic] that I would like to have my headquarter get involved, you know, to try to ensure that what we were reporting almost on a daily basis would stop. So I was asking my headquarter, do something about it; go to the appropriate Croatian authority and deal it. So it has no bearing in my view with the letter I received from General Cermak, which, if I remember, I responded immediately the same date to his letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to the letter, and what was your response, General?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, you can see it, you know. There's a -- the letter that is attached to that. Obviously, I did not agree with his comments because when I was saying, you know, about the destitute, the miserable is that there was about, from our knowledge, between 18 to 2.000 people that were left in my whole area where it used to be 80.000. They were living in village where no electricity and no running water, and General Cermak had told the IDP in my camp, you know, that if they would return to their village they would be taken care of. At the same time the looting was burning was taking place, there is also some people that we were finding, you know, that were murdered, so that did not create an environment, you know, where those people could live freely, and may I equate that to a persecution, and they had been miserable in the sense that they had the most difficulty to provide to themselves, and even though, you know, it was the end of August you could see that fall was coming, and fall in that particular area is similar to where I come from in my country, and it is very hard if you don't have the capacity to eat, yourself, or to have some form of electricity, you know, to be able to just survive. So when I receive this letter, well, I was a little bit taken off based on all the previous letter and discussions I had with General Cermak highlighting the fact that burning was taking place, that looting was taking place, that we had restriction of movement. So that's why I responded immediately to his letter, which is the one that is signed on the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Forand, you earlier mentioned a number of people that were left in the whole area. Did you say between 1.800 and 2.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's correct on the transcript, page 64, line 24. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, we have in evidence now some of the specific responses to those letters you provided, and I want to take you to one of those in a moment, but before I do --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I see I made a mistake. I said I responded on the 3rd, but it was on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, since you've mentioned that, we can turn to 65 ter 946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if anywhere in the next two to three minutes you would find a suitable moment for a break, you're invited to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could turn to -- this is a -- keep moving through that document, please, a couple of more pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a letter dated September 4th, General Forand, from you to General Cermak referencing his letter of September 3rd, 1995, and assuring him that you will receive his proof, compelling and factual proof of the burning of homes, and you'll be compiling that but meanwhile providing some immediate information about crimes taking place and asking at the last sentence: "Please investigate this most recent incident, which puts HV soldiers in the immediate vicinity of burning homes, and yet more poor farmers describe how soldiers either killed or took their means of livelihood." This is one of the responses to the -- to General Cermak's letter of September 3rd?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break at your suggestion, Mr. Tieger. I was listening to the French translation, so therefore it came a bit late for me. You were reading. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the parties have, meanwhile, received a copy of the list prepared by Mr. Registrar giving provisional exhibit numbers and 65 ter numbers for 73 documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have -- I believe it came across in the transfer of the draft form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I take it that apart from the provisional exhibit numbers that nothing has been added to this list, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that's correct. Nothing has been added to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarification, if I may. I had a discussion with Mr. Registrar about that at the break. In addition to the 73 documents, there are four documents which the Prosecution will wish to tender across the bar table that are not identified in those 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And those are not in the 73. And do they happen to be the four for which addition to your 65 ter list was granted earlier, or are they -- is it a bit from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I think they're different, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're different. These were the ones attached to the statement. You want to tender another four, and among these 73 are the four which were added to your 65 ter list. So they're part of this 73? Let me just check. We have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. Right. The -- I think -- if I understand the Court accurately, that's correct, that those are part of the 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are part of the 73. So then -- then since there are no objections --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll need them to be identified, Your Honour, which documents the Prosecution are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other four, would you say, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that this will come in a separate round of seeking them to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can do that now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to deal with these ones. Yes. Mr. Registrar, would it not be very practical that the internal memorandum in which we find the exhibit numbers together with the 65 ter numbers that that would be filed as a document so that everything is on the record?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This will be filed as a public document in the case file and distributed to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can move to a decision on the matter. That is, P334 up to and including P406 are admitted into evidence, and then we'll hear from you, Mr. Tieger, about the remaining four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether now or at any suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can raise those now just as easily and the numbers are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will not -- of course, before the Chamber admits any documents from the bar table, we would like to have a look at it so we know what we are admitting. Are the Defence teams informed about the four documents or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am not certain of exactly what we're talking about. I did have a discussion with Mr. Du-Toit about a couple of them, but consistent with Your Honours' desires and -- the Chamber's desires, if we could get the listing and look at them and just reserve our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I should mention that those were all documents, and maybe I should have indicated that as we went through them serially. They were documents that have been identified by other 65 ter numbers during the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you make a short list and give it to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if -- of course, if you say it was during the examination, then whether it's tendering through the bar table or whether it's just tendered through this witness, although, is another matter, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That was a -- oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah, just as -- on a practical level, Your Honour, going back to some of these documents, I don't -- at least we've noticed at least one of these sitreps that has come in, number 42, which is P375, it's 65 ter 1840, has been admitted already. I don't know if we are interested in avoiding the duplication of this or just letting it go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We certainly are interested in avoiding duplications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This seems to be -- almost moves into a bookkeeping session rather than -- so, Mr. Tieger, I take it that you will properly inform the Defence and that the Chamber will be informed what documents will be tendered from the bar table. Once there's clarity, we can then take the next step.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're invited now to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, thank you for your patience during what the Court accurately referred to as a bookkeeping session. Before the break, we had looked at and discussed some of the exchanges that took place toward the end of August, beginning of September 1995. I'm going to want to turn your attention in a moment to another response by you to General Cermak's 3 September letter. But before I do that, I'd like to turn your attention to the second meeting you had with General Gotovina after Operation Storm. That meeting is referred to in your statement of 2008 at paragraph 8 where you indicate that it was General Gotovina who requested that meeting, and you recall wondering at the time the reason why he wanted to meet because it seemed that he only wanted to show me his new office, and then you indicate that although it is not indicated in the sitrep for that date, I again complained about the looting and burning of houses which was occurring throughout the sector ... that this was happening but indicated that it was something could not control. It was at the conclusion of this meeting that General Gotovina threatened to kill UN Press Officer Alun Roberts for being a "spy and a provocateur." This meeting took place on 5 September 1995. Now, let me turn your attention, please, to 65 ter 3186, sir, and if we could move to the -- move three pages down. That's fine. At paragraph 6, heading Meetings With Croatian Authorities, beginning: Commander of OZ south invited commander Sector South to his recently refurbished Knin office at 1015 hours. Goes on to describe some of those present, indicates there was no stated purpose for the meeting and that General Gotovina was in an expansive mood. The second paragraph concerns General Gotovina's message about the displaced persons at the Sector South HQ camp, protesting that the UN was harbouring war criminals and grandstanding to the world media while doing so as if defending an underdog, asking that the accused be handed over to Croatian authorities and that no one could leave until that happened and asking what right the UN has to stand in judgement of the Croatian courts and noting, again, there was the now familiar justification for revenge in response to Serb actions in 1991. And then the last paragraph, addressing something that I indicated earlier when referring to your statement, and that's the references to the -- to Mr. Roberts, the Sector South press information officer, the accusation that he was a spy and provocateur and your concern about that matter and assessment that this was an attempt by General Gotovina to end press information activity in the sector and press information officer contact with the many international press. General, can you tell the Court at what point of the meeting this message was delivered by General Gotovina and your concern about the significance of that message?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. This took place -- it took me by surprise. I was accompanied by my deputy commander, Colonel Blana [phoen], and my senior liaison officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk. The meeting was completed. It was outside of his office. I was waiting to get inside my vehicle, and that's when, you know, he proffered those -- those words, you know, that he would deal with Alun Roberts. So I was completely taken aback, and I think I explained to him that in my view, Mr. Roberts, you know, was depicting exactly what was happening in the sector. And when I came back to my camp, I immediately advise UNCRO of the discussion that had taken place regarding Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to 65 ter 2840. And perhaps go an additional page. This is a letter from -- to General Cervenko, Chief of Staff of the Croatian army Zagreb from Lieutenant General Bernard Janvier advising that he had been informed by the commander of Sector South, Brigadier-General Forand that during a visit he paid to General Cermak -- it says here General Cermak in Knin on 5 September 1995, General Gotovina who was also present accused Mr. Roberts, press and information officer of the sector, of being involved in spying activities, which ultimately may justify his execution. And General Janvier goes on to express his concern about that and indicates at the last paragraph that he would very much appreciate if he could be informed about whatever measures General Cervenko deems necessary to avoid such allegations or further allegations against a member of the UN in Sector South whose commitment remains highly valued by the sector commander. General, is this a letter insofar as you're aware that followed the information you provided to headquarters about what had happened on September 5th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, I never saw that letter except there's a -- there's something that is not correct in the first paragraph. General Cermak was not there at that particular meeting, so it was only General Gotovina, myself, my deputy, and my senior liaison officer, so I don't know where General Janvier got that information. It is not certainly reflected in the sitrep that I had sent to my headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And apart from that, does the letter otherwise appear to be a response to the information you provided and the concern you expressed about what had happened on September 5th?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no reason to ask. Fairly obvious, isn't it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, one more document I want to tender across the bar table. I don't know that it's necessary to show the witness, but it's 65 ter 3319, and it's a letter from General Cervenko to General Gotovina -- well, excuse me, the other way around, a letter from General Gotovina to General Cervenko referring to General Gotovina's receipt of a warning from General Cervenko that "as commander, I am personally responsible for the treatment of members of UNCRO."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just wait --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just waiting for it to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- I had the hard copy, and it hadn't come up electronically yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I indicated a moment ago, this is a letter from General Gotovina to General Cervenko referring to his receipt on 13 September 1995 of "your warning stating that as commander I am personally responsible for the treatment of members of UNCRO in Split ZP's area of responsibility and that behaviour by members of subordinated units is inappropriate and causing serious damage to the reputation of the Croatian army as a whole, and that it conflicts directly with state policy and the positions of the leadership of the Republic of Croatia as well as with the international commitments undertaken by" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you want to tender this document from the bar table, I mean, it is follow-up correspondence, and then we'll read it, and if you read it aloud in court, then it's hardly useful anymore, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any objection against this follow-up correspondence to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I don't see any other objections. Mr. Registrar, this is not included in the list, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit P407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P407 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And a moment ago, General, I indicated that I wanted to draw your attention to one more response to General Cermak's September 3rd letter, and if I could now direct your attention to 65 ter 2256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that also not on the list, Mr. Tieger, or is this one on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you -- we will further elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. You're quite right. I am referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can now use the P number, which leaves -- also allows at later stages for links.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this letter of September 7th, 1995, that I'm referring to is P396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, P396 is a letter from you to General Cermak dated September 7th, 1995, Protest About Continued Human Rights Violations in Sector South, references to General Cermak's letter of September 3rd, 1995; your letter of 4 September 1995; your letter of 5 September 1995; and indicates that "In spite of my efforts and the efforts of other UN officials to encourage to you bring an end to the human rights violations being committed in your area of responsibility in the aftermath of Operation Storm, the burning, looting, and pillaging continues. Following the statements of the government of Croatia urging Serbs to remain in their villages, I do not understand why you are unable to put an end to the widespread and systematic destruction of the only means of subsistence available to these vulnerable victims of war. These people are not soldiers. They are totally unable to defend themselves against aggression. They depend on you for their security. They need your help, and they need it now." And you indicate on the second page that following your recent letters you wanted to make General Cermak aware of additional incidents which have occurred recently within Sector South, and you list those ... read them all out. The court can read those. I'll just continue with the end of your letter, which says: "The above incidents are illustrative of the magnitude and scope of the problem of human rights abuses in your area of responsibility. These are not unfounded allegations or insinuations without proof as you suggest in your letter 3 September. Human rights teams report what they see. What they see is not pretty. What they see is criminal, but it is the sad truth. If you are not pleased with the reports, please take action to stop the burning and the killing." Indicated this was sent to General Cermak with a -- a copy to UNCRO command, then a copy to General Gotovina, the commander, Military District South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I mean, that says commander OZ south. It doesn't say anything about General Gotovina. I mean, the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who is commander OZ south? Is there any way of agreeing -

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. There is not. That's the -- well, I would say that we've seen that reference before, but I -- that's fine. I mean, I agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that's a matter of dispute, then I take it that we will learn about it more. But perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Forand, you did send this letter? It says, copied to command OZ south. First of all, who did you intend to address when sending a copy to command OZ south?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Gotovina, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Gotovina. Have you any idea on how this was delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same way that the other were delivered. It was faxed to the military observer in Zadar and asked to be delivered to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Forand, was this a further effort by you to respond to General Cermak's letter of September 3rd and ensure to the extent you were able that these crimes were addressed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you receive a direct response from General Cermak or General Gotovina, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No. No. I never received nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We still have some time left today. Could I inquire what the sequence of cross-examination will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Cermak, I'm going to do the first cross-examination. Mr. Tieger's ended slightly shorter than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- we believed he'd be, and we haven't put our exhibits yet into a format that can be distributed by ring tail for a very good reason, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any matter you could deal with in 25 minutes so that we do not lose time in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly could as long as the parties don't mind the fact that we haven't distributed our exhibits in ring tail, but I won't be dealing with anything off-pieced, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Forand, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay, who is Defence counsel for Mr. Cermak. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First matter I'm going to ask you about is the matter of the military governor, General Forand, which was a title that you repeatedly used in relation to Mr. Cermak. Can we just look at your statement of the 19th of August, 1996, page 10, Prosecution Exhibit 330 just so that we can have a look at a description you gave in relation to General Cermak in that first statement of yours. And I'm looking at the third full paragraph in that statement. On the 6th of August, President Tudjman appointed a military governor for the sector. His name was Lieutenant-General Cermak. You gave a description there of what he was, an HV reserve officer who told me that his AOR, area of responsibility, was the whole of UN Sector South and that his job was to administer and revitalise in the newly conquered areas. He also told me that he was an artillery officer and had planned the use of artillery against the Serbs during Operation Storm. Lieutenant-General Cermak told me the above activities were -- was sweeping operations to ensure that the land was safe from Chetniks. Right. First of all, in relation to being an artillery officer, did you get that information from someone else, or are you saying that General Cermak said that to you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: As far as this paragraph is -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please answer the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes. This paragraph represents not the first meeting, but it's my recollection when I was asked a question, you know, about General Cermak, I didn't meet him on the 6th. I met him on the 7th. As I had mentioned earlier, I got the information that -- and to me it was a military governor, you know, would be coming into Knin to take over the responsibility of my area. He told me personally that he was an artillery officer many weeks afterward at a social reception that was held by the authority in Knin. It could have been three weeks to a month after the 6th of August. I don't remember exactly. It was a chat between me and him, you know, and that is where he told me he was a reserve officer, that he was an artillery, and I recall that he mentioned that he had planned the artillery plan, you know, for Operation Storm. I recall that I didn't quite believe him. I didn't tell him that I didn't believe him, but I let it go at that, and I didn't pursue further that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just letting the translation flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, you and he didn't speak the same language. You didn't speak the Croatian language. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he didn't speak English. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: He spoke a bit of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you saying he told you this in English?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, we were alone there. If he -- if I don't understand Croat and he doesn't speak English, you know -- he spoke a little bit of English, and that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that he held this conversation with you about being the artillery officer and planned the use of artillery in Operation Storm, you're saying he said that to you in English?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: That's what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, you say that's what you recall. Did you -- do you have doubts about what was said?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I don't have doubts. I recall that he said that. I don't know how else to express that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In all your meetings with him, he had someone speaking in English to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: He had a translator, and we also had a translator when we were meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you say he had a translator, was that a liaison officer between the Croatian army and the -- and you, as the UN, or an official translator?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, on his part initially it was a translator from the Croatian army, the same individual that I had seen the first time I had met with General Gotovina. And after that, I don't remember if that individual was there all the time, but we were also bringing our own translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just help me to identify who that person is, if you can. Who was the translator? Did you get to know the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there liaison officers who were in fact speaking to you in English when you had meetings with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: You mean liaison officer from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Croatian. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Like I said, initially there was one individual that I remember his face because I had seen him the first time that I went to see General Gotovina with General Kotil. I don't remember if he stayed there throughout all the meetings that I had with General Cermak, but there was somebody that was doing the translation for General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, there seems to be some -- a bit of confusion. I think the witness earlier told us that the person he saw also in a meeting with General Gotovina, that he then called him a translator, and now it appears that when you're asking about liaison officers that he is referring to the same person. So there might be some confusion, and you're invited to seek clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and that is the point of this questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had as commander of UNCRO liaison officers from the Croatian army dealing with the UNCRO forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, first, I was not the commander of UNCRO. I was commander of Sector South --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: -- which was part of UNCRO. There were certain individuals that were liaison officer. Captain Lukovic, you know, was an individual with whom we were doing liaison with, but there was other people. I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As commander of Sector South, you had regular dealings or your forces had regular dealings with the Croatian army liaison officers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Not quite because that's one of the problem that we were encountering is that on the Croat side the only liaison that was taking place was taking place at my level. My battalion commander could not have a liaison with the Croat authority. It was always elevated at my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that liaison officer from the Croatian army would be dealing with you personally. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, not with me. He was dealing with my officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that -- I thought you said that problem was they'd only be dealing at your level.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: My level in the sense that my headquarter, not with the unit level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. So the liaison officer of the Croatian army with whom you or your subordinates were dealing with was someone whom you had regular contact with concerning the activities of the Croatian army forces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, the way it was organised, I had a Senior Liaison Officer who was Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk. He was the one that was doing the liaison on my part. He was the one that organised meeting, you know, was aware of when the meeting -- if General Cermak wanted to have a meeting, then we coordinate. It was through Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk. Then I was made aware that a meeting was requested, or if I requested a meeting it was through Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk who went to General Cermak headquarter to request a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Taking as an example in your statement in a passage, you refer to a message on the 4th of August from a marine Lukovic about keeping radio silence during Operation Storm. Do you recollect that passage?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that the liaison officer, Lukovic, who was passing that information to you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: It was from whom we received it. It was signed by him, that particular letter, you know, advising us to that we should stop transmitting because in his view we were passing information to the other side, and we would be dealt with if we continue to provide that particular information. But it was the en-tete - I don't know what's the word in English - the heading was for the government of Croatia, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And those liaison officers were the point of contact for your forces in dealing with military issues. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was also some military observer that were co-located at the headquarter of General Gotovina, which was in Zadar, and that's how I transmitted the letter, you know, that I sent to General Gotovina on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were aware that the liaison officers in Zadar had a superior in Zagreb, a Brigadier Plestina who was their superior in relation to the exchange through the liaison officers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware -- I remember that I met the Brigadier Plestina when he came to visit my headquarter in Knin, and that's where I learned that he was the liaison officer at UNCRO level. But before that, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your knowledge of the structure of the liaison officers and where they reported was not detailed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: It was sufficient that when I sent something through my -- through the military observer that I was guaranteed that it was delivered to the individual that would give it to the person that I was sending to. And when I had, again, that first meeting with General Gotovina with General Kotil, Captain Lukovic was also present at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He was a naval captain, Lukovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I think I remember, yeah, that he was called captain and captain naval, yes. He was a marine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he also spoke English. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, he did speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But not English to a fluent level. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: I'm the wrong person to ask about fluency, but he was speaking English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, you're the only person there --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, but sufficient for me to understand. Now, am I considered fluent? You know, I think we have the same approach. We understand; we can argue; we can exchange information with sufficient, I think, detail that we understand what we're meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are we to take the terms of your evidence this morning that you say it was the suggestion of a military observer in Zadar that a military governor for the region was to be appointed? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yeah. What I recall is either Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk or Major Balfour, who was my senior ops officer, told me that he got -- he had received information from a military observer that was at Zadar that he they would be a military governor that would be appoint for their region of Knin. That's how I learned that somebody that -- from the Croat authority would be coming, you know, to become in charge with, and that would be the person with who eventually we would be dealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to help me as to who this military observer was, who gave this information about a military governor?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, sorry, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any other details that might help me find him, locate him?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, if Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk or Major Balfour comes as a witness, I suppose you could ask them, but I don't remember myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The first information we have about a military governor according to these papers is a letter written by you, in fact, on the 5th of August. Shall we just have a look at that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That letter is a Prosecution Exhibit from this morning, so I'm unable to tie up, Your Honour, what number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have the 65 ter number, it might be easy to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It has been given -- I can give you the number. R0038166.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might assist Mr. Registrar. We not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That must be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the letter you wrote to General Gotovina. "I urgently request a meeting with the military governor of the region." What did you understand a military governor to mean?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, to me, it was the individual that was responsible for the area to deal with any matter, you know, that may surface that would be of interest to me as the Sector South commander, whether it pertained to military aspect or humanitarian aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that would be a political appointment by the Croatian government to that position. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, you know, the way that it was appointed. To me it was somebody to whom I could go, you know, and have discussion and to ensure that whatever problem we were facing, you know, he would -- I hope that he would be in a position to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know whether the position of military governor actually existed within the Croatian legal system or constitutional system?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this a matter that you referred to your UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb to assist you with -- in having a military governor to help you with your problems?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No, except that all the situation report and the letter that I wrote to General Cermak, you know, was titled Military Governor of Knin, and nobody ever came back to tell me that that was not the proper title that I should use, and I did not ask my headquarter at UNCRO to tell me, you know, what the military governor should do or should not do or what were the responsibility or if it was applicable because they receive, also, the same information, and nobody ever came back to tell me that I should not use that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Cermak never wrote to you under the title of military governor, did he?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He always wrote to you as the commander of the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, let's say "always" is a big word because I think I received three letters from him compared to 12 or 15 that I sent him, which was addressed as the military governor of the Knin region. But, you're right. The -- from what I recall, it was not written as military governor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So were you aware that you were giving him an incorrect title, an incorrect rank?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: No. In my view, you know, the first time I had met him on the 7th, he had told me that he was responsible for the Knin region, and to me, you know, if you're responsible, then that entails everything that happens goes through you. And when I went to see General Gotovina on the 6th, he told me to refer any matters to General Cermak, so to me that was sufficient. And in addition when we start to have our meeting with General Cermak, he was always indicating -- well, most of the time indicating that he would deal with the matter that was brought to him, whether they were in Knin or outside of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were told to refer any problems you may have to him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. You, being a part of the UN forces in the region. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Yes, because I was the Sector South commander. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And -- we'll look a little bit further at other evidence concerning this tomorrow, but is it correct that the Canadian Forces as part of the UN forces had particular problems down in this region during Operation Storm because some of your troops had been taken into custody or detention by Croatian army troops?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND
utterances.text: Well, obviously there were some problem because some troops, you know, were threatened to get out of their observation posts, but you will see also in sitrep that was sent to UNCRO that it is clearly reflected that those taken to Zadar were well taken care by the Croat troops, and none of the Canadian, you know, suffered any casualty until a couple of their observation posts received some artillery fire. The contention was the fact that some equipment initially were denied to the Canadian to take with them when they were vacating their posts. But I would suggest that there would have been more problem with the Czech battalion who lost two people and that the four people that were seriously wounded or the Kenyans battalion that got an individual that was killed in that, three or four individuals that were also wounded, so I would not single out the Canadian as the one of the unit that had major problem with that particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock. It is a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have asked you two minutes before to find a suitable moment, but I was at that moment busy with another matter. That is, you said in relation to this 65 ter number 1612 that you -- that was a document that was dealt with this morning. I went through this list and didn't find it. I then went to e-court and find no exhibit number finally assigned. So it appears that it's a new document. It is not, then I would like someone to assist me in -- because in the e-court system, no exhibit number has been assigned. It does not appear on this morning's list. That's the list prepared by Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is probably a duplicate, Your Honour. We have this problem with documents with duplicate or triplicates or quadruplicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We sometimes have a document with that number on that causes our work in progress and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the parties will have until tomorrow morning, 9.00, to help me out with this problem because, Mr. Forand, we will adjourn for the day. We will continue tomorrow morning. But before we adjourn, and this might be a conversation which is more interesting to you than some of the previous ones, time estimates. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Up to six hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Up to six hours. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Probably about four, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Mikulicic or Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At least two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That makes 12 together. Effective, we have approximately four hours a day. I'm looking at you at this moment, Mr. Forand, because this means that the parties would like to put questions to you for at least quite a number of more days. Three days is what is more or less expected. You're prepared for that? I mean, I don't know your schedule.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm here, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes we hear that witnesses have to leave very quickly and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I will organise myself, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will organise yourself. Thank you very much for this flexibility. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Document is 1654.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1654. That's -- yes. We will try to find it on the list. Mr. Tieger. You are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just going to say it is now P347, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P347. Okay. Everything is now on the record. We will adjourn for the day. Mr. Forand, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00; however, not in this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, I think it was in Courtroom II -- Courtroom III where we meet tomorrow, and I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether the testimony already given or testimony still to be given. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00.
